claim: Moving an established statistical analysis to another programming language requires preserving parameter conventions, observation models, and numerical behavior as well as equations. HGFX provides hierarchical Gaussian filtering in Python, targeting a frozen MATLAB HGF Toolbox 8.2.0 reference while removing MATLAB from the user runtime. We describe the statistical contract, fitting workflow, and evaluation of the released HGFX 1.0.0 package. Configuration and numerical checks are complemented by paired workflow, recovery, and backend experiments. MATLAB and HGFX select the same Bayesian information criterion winner in all 36 frozen model-selection cases, while both achieve generating-model recovery balanced accuracy of 0.583. Parameter-recovery criteria are not fully met. A separate trial-horizon experiment fails its paired-integrity gate and cannot support a stronger identifiability conclusion. A comparison with pyhgf 0.3.2 establishes agreement for 11 mapped perceptual quantities in one three-level binary case; participant-response negative log-likelihood remains not directly comparable. Retained Tesla T4 evidence supports objective agreement in tested fitting cells, without establishing a speed advantage. Source audits of two published applications identify unresolved custom-model requirements and do not yield an executed real-data replication. The contribution is a reference-compatible software workflow with explicit boundaries: reproducibility across implementations does not establish parameter identifiability, model discrimination, or validity for a new experimental design.

claim: The Hierarchical Gaussian Filter (HGF) describes learning about states whose uncertainty and volatility change over time [@mathys2011; @mathys2014]. It combines a hierarchical generative model with approximate inference that updates beliefs after each observation. Applications include studies of prediction errors and social learning [@iglesias2013; @diaconescu2014]. The MATLAB implementation associated with TAPAS supplies model configurations, fitting, simulation and diagnostic workflows [@fraessle2021tapas]. These supporting conventions matter to an applied analysis because they determine which quantities are estimated and how the resulting evidence is calculated.

claim: Numerical evaluation adds another layer. The HGF is recursive, so a local discrepancy can propagate through later beliefs. Fitting adds derivatives, optimizer stopping decisions and curvature calculations. Agreement of a fixed-parameter trajectory is therefore necessary evidence for a fitting comparison, but it does not imply identical fitted parameters. Conversely, a fitted endpoint discrepancy does not locate the underlying cause. It may reflect a changed observation model, a different transform, a numerical derivative, or sensitivity within the reference implementation. These possibilities require distinct checks rather than a single correlation between output vectors. General guidance on computational modeling likewise distinguishes implementation checks from recovery and substantive inference [@wilson2019ten], within the broader requirement for computational reproducibility [@peng2011reproducible].

claim: Belief inference and parameter optimization solve different problems. The filter produces a trajectory conditional on parameters; maximum a posteriori optimization searches for parameters using the likelihood and priors. Curvature at the fitted solution then supports the documented approximate covariance and Laplace evidence calculations. Bayesian information criterion (BIC) uses the negative log likelihood, free-parameter count and reference observation count; it is not the negative log joint. The evaluation consequently checks objective components and statistical outputs separately. No new inferential method is proposed here.
